GUEST ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICIAL REPORTS: 
MAYOR: Robert “Bo” Bemmes: 
National Night Out and Police Services 
The city’s police department held its seventh consecutive National Night Out at Caney Park. The event provides an 
opportunity for residents to learn about public safety resources and for local law enforcement agencies to strengthen 
relationships and mutual-aid partnerships. 
Residents can see demonstrations and equipment from the police department and neighboring agencies, including K9 units 
and drones.

Residents are also reminded not to leave valuables in their vehicles. Valuables should be taken inside, secured in the trunk, 
or, at minimum, vehicles should be locked. 
Reading Road Water Main Replacement 
The Safety and Services Department, Public Works Department, and city engineers are continuing to discuss the replacement 
of water mains along Reading Road, from the city’s northern corporation line to the southern corporation line. The need for 
the project became more apparent during discussions surrounding the proposed Reading Road road diet, which will not move 
forward. Preliminary estimates indicate that the project could cost more than $4 million. The city will provide additional 
information once final costs are determined and will then address financing options. 
Veterans Memorial Stadium 
Veterans Memorial Stadium is scheduled to host 87 games or events over a 93-day period. The heavy schedule reinforces the 
city’s interest in eventually installing artificial turf, which would allow the facility to be used more extensively throughout 
the year. Artificial turf could potentially expand usage from roughly two months and 100 events annually to year-round use 
and more than 1,000 events, providing additional opportunities for youth activities and athletics. 
New Track Project 
The city is accepting bids for a new track at Veterans Memorial Stadium. The project is supported by a $350,000 State of 
Ohio grant that must be used within the next year. The grant is not sufficient to fund improvements such as new bleachers or 
artificial turf, but it will allow the city to move forward with installation of a new track. The city will determine the project's 
final scope after receiving the bids. 
Crestmont and West Crest Water Main Project 
A pre-construction meeting has been held for the East Crest, Crestmont, and West Crest improvements, including the portion 
of West Crest from Keith Drive to Crestmont. Construction is expected to begin shortly after January 5. The city 
intentionally avoided starting the project late in the fall to prevent construction from extending through the winter and 
holiday season, as occurred with the Maple Drive project. The project includes significant water main improvements that 
will benefit residents and the fire department. The city will provide updates as construction progresses. 
Future Ronald Reagan Highway Closure 
ODOT has notified the city of a major future project involving the closure of Ronald Reagan Highway from Galbraith Road 
to Plainfield Road. The closure is expected to last approximately four to six months and is currently anticipated for 2030. 
There will be additional review and planning before the project begins, and the city will keep residents informed. The project 
is expected to create significant disruption for the community. 
Waste and Recycling Contract 
The city's waste and recycling contract expires at the end of the year. The city is preparing bid specifications and will work 
with the appropriate committee to determine whether services should be changed, added, or eliminated in the next contract. 
Lead Service Line Notifications 
The city is working with the Water Department to update notification procedures required by the EPA concerning lead 
service lines and lines for which the material is unknown. The new requirements create additional administrative 
responsibilities for the Water Department, requiring employees to spend more time on documentation and recordkeeping. 
The city is working to provide the department with the necessary assistance while continuing its regular water infrastructure 
work. 
Health Insurance Savings 
The city will soon conduct its annual health insurance review. This marks the city's 12th year participating in a self-insured 
group through the Ohio Benefits Cooperative. Over the past 12 years, the average premium renewal increase has been 
approximately 4.79%, compared with increases of 15% to 20% experienced by other communities. The city estimates that 
participation in the cooperative has saved more than $1 million over that period.

Mayor Bemmes credited Safety and Services Director Patrick Ross with significant work in managing the program and 
controlling costs. Health insurance had previously experienced annual increases of 18% to 20%, making the cooperative a 
substantial financial benefit to the city. 
Traffic Safety 
The city recorded 35 automobile accidents during July. Mayor Bemmes emphasized that this number is too high and that the 
city must continue looking for ways to improve traffic safety and reduce crashes. 
E-Bike Safety and Enforcement 
The city continues to receive concerns regarding electric bicycles and the various classifications and regulations that apply to 
them. Mayor Bemmes noted that many of the applicable laws have been on the books for decades. The purpose of 
enforcement is not to unnecessarily restrict residents but to protect riders and others from potentially dangerous situations. 
Police officers may intervene when they believe a person is in danger, and the same principle applies to young people riding 
e-bikes. The goal is to ensure that everyone gets home safely. The city will continue reviewing e-bike concerns with the 
appropriate committee. 
Flock Camera Technology 
The city addressed concerns surrounding Flock license plate recognition cameras. Reading currently has four Flock cameras. 
The police department uses the technology as an investigative and public safety tool while seeking to protect individual 
privacy. The system is not continuously monitored and is not intended for continuous surveillance. Information is shared only 
when there is a legitimate law enforcement or public safety purpose. 
Flock cameras can assist with: 
• Investigating criminal activity 
• Identifying vehicles associated with incidents 
• Recovering stolen vehicles 
• Locating wanted individuals 
• Assisting in the recovery of missing or endangered children and at-risk adults 
• Providing real-time alerts involving vehicles on validated hotlists 
The cameras detect license plates. They do not use facial recognition or identify people based on gender or race. According 
to the city's stated policies, Flock data is restricted to official law enforcement purposes. Its use for immigration 
enforcement, traffic enforcement, harassment, intimidation, or targeting individuals based on race, sex, or religion is 
prohibited. Mayor Bemmes stated that the technology has been helpful to the city and does not believe its use constitutes an 
invasion of residents' privacy. 
Property Maintenance and Code Enforcement 
The city's exterior property maintenance code enforcement officer continues to play an important role in addressing property- 
related concerns. The city has strengthened coordination among code enforcement, the Fire Department, Board of Health, 
and Building Department. Residents with property maintenance concerns are encouraged to contact the Safety and Services 
Director or Assistant Fire Chief. The goal is to allow the code enforcement officer to spend less time answering phones and 
more time addressing problems in the community. Mayor Bemmes praised the officer's performance and the effectiveness of 
the coordinated approach.

Katie Eadicicco: 
Clarifying E-Bike Classifications 
Discussed continued confusion surrounding e-bikes and the distinctions between e-bikes, motorbikes, mini bikes, dirt bikes, 
and e-scooters. There was particular concern that residents may not understand which types of bikes are permitted on public 
roads and which are subject to age, helmet, or other restrictions. It was noted that the city’s committee has already been

CITY OF READING, OHIO

reviewing the issue, along with the Safety and Services Department and Police Department. Council requested that the 
committee continue researching the matter and report back with additional clarification. 
State Law and Local Regulations 
A key concern is the potential confusion between the Ohio Revised Code and the city's existing regulations. It was 
emphasized that many of the applicable requirements are established by state law and cannot simply be overridden by the 
city. Council agreed that clearer information would benefit residents, particularly families purchasing e-bikes for children. 
One council member noted that Class 3 e-bikes can travel up to 28 miles per hour and are subject to age and helmet 
requirements. State law also requires e-bikes to display a label identifying their classification, which should make the 
different classes easier to distinguish. It was also clarified that dirt bikes are generally not permitted on public roads and 
must be operated on private property with permission. 
Public Education and Online Resources 
Council discussed creating or expanding educational materials on the city's website and social media platforms. Visual 
information, including photographs showing the differences among e-bikes, dirt bikes, mini bikes, and other types of 
motorized bicycles, could help residents understand the regulations. It was indicated that some information may already be 
available on the city's website and agreed to review the existing materials to determine whether additional or clearer 
information is needed. 
Council members also referenced similar educational information recently published by police departments in neighboring 
communities, including Mariemont, Blue Ash, Evendale, and Sharonville. The information from those communities generally 
reflects the requirements of the Ohio Revised Code. 
Youth Safety and Education 
Council discussed the possibility of connecting families with organizations that offer bicycle or e-bike safety classes for 
children. Because e-bikes are becoming increasingly popular, officials agreed that safety education could be beneficial. 
However, it was explained that staffing limitations make it difficult for the city's police department to conduct its own classes 
at this time. Outside organizations or existing community programs may provide a more practical option. 
Key Takeaways 
• The city will continue reviewing e-bike classifications and applicable regulations. 
• Officials will clarify the relationship between local rules and the Ohio Revised Code. 
• Existing city website and social media information will be reviewed and expanded if necessary. 
• Educational materials with photographs and clear descriptions could help residents distinguish between different 
types of bikes. 
• Parents are encouraged to understand an e-bike's classification and legal requirements before purchasing one for a 
child. 
• Class 3 e-bikes can reach speeds of up to 28 mph and have specific age and helmet requirements. 
• E-bikes are required to display a classification label under state law. 
• Dirt bikes generally cannot be operated on public roads and must be used on private property with permission.
